verdict_reasoning: The goal is reasonable, and the cost stays inside pgbench on platforms without ppoll(). The thread has not settled whether a larger select() fd set would lift the limit with less code (maintenance-fit-2); message #7 answers that alternative without a prototype or a size. The kqueue path also replaces select() at every client count, with a -4% result on one laptop (prior-attempts-1), and no test guards its kernel state (maintenance-fit-1). Demand is thin but did not stop the review (demand-1).

brief.title: pgbench: kqueue implementation of the socket set on macOS
brief.problem: pgbench falls back to select() on platforms without ppoll(), such as macOS, so one pgbench process cannot wait on more than 1024 sockets (FD_SETSIZE). The author needs many more clients than threads to test connection overhead and pool management in connection poolers.
brief.proposed_design: The patch adds a third socket_set implementation in pgbench.c based on kqueue(), used where kqueue(2) exists and ppoll(2) does not. Because kqueue registrations persist in the kernel, wait_on_socket_set() disables stale registrations, enables the current set and maps events back to input slots through udata. v2 skips the disable step when the fd set has not changed since the previous wait.
user_visible_surface: pgbench on macOS and similar platforms accepts more than about 1024 clients per thread; no new option or syntax.
author_claims: Removes the FD_SETSIZE limit of 1024 clients for pgbench on macOS.
v2 matches select() throughput wherever select() can run, within about -4% to +4% tps on the author's laptop.
v1 lost about 5-8% tps against select() at small client counts because of an extra kevent() call per wait.
Worst-case cost of stale-fd cleanup is O(nregistered * nclosed), mainly when all clients close at once.
The design follows the existing kqueue use in the backend wait event code (waiteventset.c).
brief.thread_state: Kirill Reshke supports it and tested it on macOS; Yura Sokolov says pgbench has wider O(n) per-wakeup costs. Jeff Anton argues that redefining FD_SETSIZE or a custom bit array is simpler, and the author replied with objections that nobody has answered yet.
unclear: Whether the patch changes configure or meson to detect kqueue, since only pgbench.c is touched.
Which platforms besides macOS would select the kqueue path, and whether any were tested.
Whether pgbench documentation mentions the client limit per platform and needs an update.
How the patch handles the -C reconnect case where a closed fd is reused for a new connection, beyond the author's reasoning.
Whether Windows, which also lacks ppoll(), stays on select().

prior_attempts.title: pgbench - option to build using ppoll() for larger connection counts
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P16 used ppoll() to lift the pgbench connection limit, and pgbench now uses ppoll() where it exists. This patch adds kqueue only for platforms that lack ppoll().

prior_attempts.title: kqueue
prior_attempts.quote: Degraded performance for clients on the same machine does seem to be a show stopper for this patch for now.
prior_attempts.reason: Benchmarks gave mixed results: kqueue helped on macOS and on large bare-metal FreeBSD servers with remote clients, but it was slower on NetBSD and on FreeBSD virtual machines when pgbench ran on the same machine. Neither the author nor the testers found the cause. The author called the slowdown for local clients a show stopper and was still asking kernel developers about it when the entry was returned.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P5 put kqueue in the server's WaitEventSet; this patch puts kqueue in pgbench only. The performance finding in P5 concerns the server and does not carry over to this patch.

objections.title: Lifting the select() limit may not need a third socket set
objections.failure_scenario: The project adds and keeps a third wait implementation in pgbench for one platform. A heap-allocated fd_set, or _DARWIN_UNLIMITED_SELECT on macOS, could raise the same 1024 cap with a small change to the existing select() path. Every later socket_set change then has to be written and checked three times.
objections.argument: Message #6 proposes raising FD_SETSIZE or using a private bit array. Message #7 says that alternative would be fragile and about as large, but gives no size or prototype. The O(max_fd) cost it cites does not matter at the client counts pgbench reaches. A committer would likely want the smaller change ruled out with evidence before adding stateful, platform-specific code, and the stated need is one tester running connection-pooler tests on a laptop (messages #2 and #4).
objections.author_must_show: How large is a select()-based fix using a dynamically sized fd_set or _DARWIN_UNLIMITED_SELECT, and what does it fail to do that the kqueue set does?

critic.reasoning: Message #7 answers the select() alternative with questions and an O(max_fd) cost it calls not critical, without a prototype or size. The alternative can do the job on macOS, so the comparison is still open.

objections.title: Default macOS pgbench runs may get slower to serve the over-1024 case
objections.failure_scenario: A developer benchmarks a patch on macOS with pgbench -c 32 -j 1 against a local server. After this change pgbench uses kqueue for every run, so the client measures up to about 4% fewer tps. The developer may count the drop against the server patch, since nothing in the output shows the wait method changed.
objections.argument: In [P5], kqueue was returned partly because it was slower when pgbench ran on the same machine as the server. Message #8 shows v2 at -4% for -c 32 -j 1, from medians of 3-4 runs on one macOS laptop. The gain in this patch is functional and only matters above 1024 clients, but per message #1 the kqueue path replaces select() for all client counts. pgbench is itself a measuring tool, so any change in its own overhead shifts results for every macOS user.
objections.author_must_show: Does kqueue stay within noise of select() on a second macOS machine and at low client counts, or should select() stay the default below FD_SETSIZE?

critic.reasoning: Message #8 shows -4% at -c 32 -j 1 from one laptop, and the kqueue path replaces select() for all client counts on macOS. P5 concerns the server's WaitEventSet and must not be used as support.

objections.title: Stateful kqueue path keeps a pgbench invariant that only macOS exercises
objections.failure_scenario: A later patch changes how threadRun adds or drops client sockets, perhaps the O(n) rework suggested in messages #3 and #5. It passes on Linux with ppoll(). On macOS a stale or reused-fd knote then misses events or reports them to the wrong slot, and pgbench hangs or miscounts under -C. Only a macOS user running many clients finds it.
objections.argument: select() and ppoll() rebuild the set on every wait, so the rest of pgbench can ignore their state. The kqueue set keeps kernel registrations across calls, and v2 also skips the disable step when the fd set looks unchanged. Its correctness for -C rests on the kernel reusing fd numbers (message #5). Nothing fails on the main development platforms if a future change breaks that, and the thread shows testing only on two laptops, with a client count above 512 never measured.
objections.author_must_show: Which test, run on the buildfarm's macOS animals, would fail if a later pgbench change broke the kqueue set's view of added, closed or reused sockets?

critic.reasoning: The kqueue set keeps kernel registrations across waits, and message #5 rests the -C case on the kernel reusing fd numbers. The thread names no test that would fail on macOS if a later change broke this.

objections.title: Demand for more than 1024 pgbench clients on macOS is not shown
objections.failure_scenario: The project adds a third socket_set path to pgbench that only macOS and BSD builds use. Few people run more than 1024 clients from a Mac, so bugs in the stateful kqueue path, such as fd reuse under -C, can go unnoticed for several releases. The pgbench maintainers then debug code that few developers can run or reproduce.
objections.argument: The only stated user is the author, who wants to stress-test connection poolers from a laptop (messages #1, #4). The only supporter calls the case "uncommon" (message #2). The other large-client user in the thread runs with -j equal to -c, which points to Linux hosts where ppoll() already removes the limit (message #3). Two workarounds exist: run pgbench on Linux, or start several pgbench processes. The proposal does not say why these fail for pooler testing.
objections.author_must_show: Who besides the author drives more than 1024 clients from one pgbench process on macOS or BSD, and why do Linux hosts or several pgbench processes not work for them?

critic.reasoning: The thread shows one user with this need on macOS, and message #2 calls the case uncommon. P6 asked for a speed gain in the server and must not be used as support; FreeBSD has ppoll(), so the path is mostly macOS.

refuted.title: Several pgbench processes already exceed 1024 connections on macOS
refuted.failure_scenario: A pooler developer on macOS needs 4000 client connections with few threads. Today they can start four pgbench processes with -c 1000 -j 1 each and add up the results. The patch saves that step but adds a third socket_set implementation that is tested mainly on one platform.
refuted.argument: FD_SETSIZE limits descriptor numbers per process, so splitting the load across processes works now. Message #4 needs clients far above threads in total, and that fits this workaround. The cost is manual aggregation and unsynchronized start, which makes it less convenient but still workable. The precedent for the Windows select() limit drew the suggestion to document the limit, though that reason is an AI summary.
refuted.author_must_show: Which pooler tests need one pgbench process with more than 1024 clients, and why do several processes with aggregated results not give a usable measurement?

precedents.title: pgbench stopped supporting large number of client connections on Windows

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of demand-1, which already asks why several pgbench processes do not work. P3 was closed because its author stopped responding, so it gives little support.

refuted.title: A larger select() fd set may be smaller than a kqueue path
refuted.failure_scenario: Later changes to the socket_set interface must update three implementations, and the kqueue one carries persistent kernel state, stale-registration cleanup and fd-reuse handling. A mistake in the -C reconnect path shows up as hangs or missed events, and only macOS users would see it.
refuted.argument: Message #6 proposes keeping the select() path and enlarging the fd set, for example through FD_SETSIZE or a custom bit array. Message #7 answers that this is fragile at compile time, costs O(max_fd), and would need Darwin-specific handling such as _DARWIN_UNLIMITED_SELECT. Nobody has replied to that answer. Message #5 already shows the stateful kqueue design needs reasoning about fd reuse that the stateless options do not need.
refuted.author_must_show: How large is a select() variant with a dynamically sized fd set on macOS, and what does it fail to do that the kqueue path does?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of maintenance-fit-2, which asks the same question about a select() variant with a larger fd set.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The patch adds a third, stateful socket_set implementation in pgbench.c that only platforms without ppoll() use.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: The kqueue path replaces select() in the pgbench wait loop at every client count on macOS.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: A larger select() fd set or several pgbench processes may already cover the stated need.

questions: How large is a select()-based fix using a dynamically sized fd_set or _DARWIN_UNLIMITED_SELECT, and what does it fail to do that the kqueue set does?
Does kqueue stay within noise of select() on a second macOS machine at low client counts, or should select() stay the default below FD_SETSIZE?
Which test on the buildfarm's macOS animals would fail if a later pgbench change broke the kqueue set's view of added, closed or reused sockets?
Who besides the author drives more than 1024 clients from one pgbench process on macOS, and why do several pgbench processes not work for them?
How does the build detect kqueue when the patch touches only pgbench.c, and which platforms besides macOS take the kqueue path?

committability.owner_note: It needs a committer who knows the pgbench threadRun loop and kqueue behaviour on macOS; nobody in the visible thread is identified as one.
committability.liability: The owner signs for a stateful wait path that only macOS-like platforms exercise, including fd reuse under -C, for as long as pgbench supports platforms without ppoll().
committability.author_follow_up: The author answered the select() alternative in message #7 and posted v2 with measurements in message #8, both within two weeks of the first post.

priority.reason: The patch is one 8.8 KB change to pgbench.c for users who run more than 1024 clients per pgbench process on macOS. The choice between kqueue and a larger select() fd set should be settled before code review.

provisional_note: Without the code, the -C fd reuse handling, the v2 rule for skipping the disable step, and the kqueue build detection could not be checked. The numbers in message #8 come from one laptop and are taken from the reviewers' reports.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Extend pgbench partitioning to pgbench_history
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes pgbench's --partitions option also partition pgbench_history, using the same method as pgbench_accounts. It adds no separate option to turn this on or off.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author did not answer Melanie Plageman's review for about three months, so Robert Haas returned the entry with feedback. She asked why the history table should be partitioned by account ID rather than by time, and why tellers and branches were left out. She also said the doc text wrongly implies that the pgbench_history partitions are created with equal sizes.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Since there has been no response to these review comments for more
than 3 months, I have set https://commitfest.postgresql.org/48/4679/
to Returned with Feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: pgbench allow '=' in \set
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Robert Haas, Tom Lane, Pavel Stehule
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch let pgbench ignore an optional leading '=' in a \set expression, so that `\set id = 1 + ...` would mean the same as `\set id 1 + ...`. The goal was readability of the expression syntax recently added to pgbench.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Robert Haas objected to optional noise words: in LOCK TABLE, the optional TABLE keyword created parser ambiguities that blocked LOCK VIEW and similar syntax for years. He added that the '=' only restates what \set already says. Earlier, Pavel Stehule said it breaks consistency with psql, and Tom Lane said it adds inconsistency in pgbench itself. The author then marked the entry rejected.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Generally, I don't like optional noise words.

precedents_retrieved.title: pgbench stopped supporting large number of client connections on Windows
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes the socket checks in pgbench and in the parallel code of reindexdb and vacuumdb so that Windows can use more than about 90 client connections or jobs. On Windows, socket values can be at or above FD_SETSIZE even when few sockets are in use, so the patch checks the fd_set count instead of the socket value.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author stopped responding, and the entry stayed "Waiting on Author" across several commitfests until it was closed. Fabien COELHO objected that the patch relies on the internals of the Windows fd_set structure, which an earlier version had been rejected for. David Steele suggested the problem is a limitation that could be documented instead of fixed.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Now your patch is basically resurrecting that. Why not if there is no other solution, but this is quite depressing, and because it breaks the interface it would be broken if windows changed its internals for some reason:-(

precedents_retrieved.title: kqueue
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a kqueue implementation of the WaitEventSet API for macOS and the BSDs, beside the existing epoll and poll implementations. A later version uses EVFILT_PROC to detect postmaster death instead of the postmaster pipe, and the author proposed building NetBSD with WAIT_USE_POLL.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Benchmarks gave mixed results: kqueue helped on macOS and on large bare-metal FreeBSD servers with remote clients, but it was slower on NetBSD and on FreeBSD virtual machines when pgbench ran on the same machine. Neither the author nor the testers found the cause. The author called the slowdown for local clients a show stopper and was still asking kernel developers about it when the entry was returned.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Degraded performance for clients on the same machine does seem to be a show stopper for this patch for now.

precedents_retrieved.title: kqueue support for WaitEventSet
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a kqueue-based implementation of WaitEventSet for BSD-family systems and macOS, as an alternative to poll(). The goal was better scalability on many-CPU machines, similar to the epoll gain on Linux.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Heikki Linnakangas ran pgbench on a 40-core FreeBSD 10.3 machine, found no performance difference against poll(), and returned the patch until someone posts results that show a benefit. Tom Lane agreed that platform-specific code costs more to maintain and needs a measurable gain, and noted that Thomas could not measure one either. After the decision, Tom measured a 5-7% gain on macOS, which he said needed reproduction. Marko Tiikkaja's concern about treating EINTR as success on older BSDs was also open.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I'm marking this as "Returned with Feedback", waiting for someone to
post test results that show a positive performance benefit from this.

precedents_retrieved.title: automatic client-side column-level encryption
precedents_retrieved.summary: Columns marked as encrypted are encrypted and decrypted by the client (libpq), so the server only stores ciphertext in new pg_encrypted_* types. Column encryption keys are catalog objects wrapped by client-held column master keys and sent to clients through new protocol messages behind a _pq_.column_encryption extension.
precedents_retrieved.objection: No closing message is shown, so the visible messages do not state the final reason. The patch stalled in 2023 after extra pg_attribute columns caused a measurable printtup slowdown. After the 2024 rebase, Jelte Fennema-Nio objected that a column encryption key cannot be rotated online, and Robert Haas questioned adding encryption fields to RowDescription and ParameterDescription for every column. The thread ends with no author reply to these points.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: So, I feel quite strongly that shipping the proposed feature without being able to re-encrypt columns in an online fashion would be a mistake.

precedents_retrieved.title: Batched clock sweep to reduce cross-socket atomic contention
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch has each backend claim a batch of consecutive buffer IDs (up to 64) from nextVictimBuffer with one atomic fetch-add, then sweep them privately, to cut cross-socket contention on that cache line. Later versions sized the batch by CPU and NUMA topology, and added a separate patch that replaces the 0..5 usage_count with a 1-bit HOT/COOL evictor.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew it after benchmarking Tomas Vondra's NUMA partitioned clock sweep patchset, which beat the batched sweep on both test machines. Andres Freund had argued from the start that a partitioned sweep was the better design. He also said batching that ignores per-backend replacement rates leaves batches held by slow backends undecremented, and that the benchmarks used an all-in-page-cache setup with no real IO. The HOT/COOL evictor moved to the NUMA thread.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: It solves a problem that partitioning solves better and more generally, and I see no argument for carrying a second mechanism for the same cache line.

precedents_retrieved.title: socket_timeout in interfaces/libpq
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a socket_timeout connection parameter to libpq so a client stops waiting and disconnects when a non-functional, overloaded server stops responding. The timeout was to be enforced inside pqWait(), the point where libpq clients can wait without end.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier said earlier reviewers did not like an option that forces a cancellation on the connection. He also objected that a timeout in pqWait() skips the cleanup that pqDropConnection() normally does, since pqWait() is written never to time out. Reviewers did not engage further, and David Steele returned the patch, which no longer applied and still had no consensus.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Just with a quick look, assuming that you can bypass all
cleanup operations normally taken by pqDropConnection() through a
hijacking of pqWait() is not fine as this routine explicitely assumes
to *never* have a timeout for its wait.

precedents_retrieved.title: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO SELECT [FOR ...]
precedents_retrieved.summary:
INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO SELECT [FOR ...]
Threads: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO SELECT [FOR ...] take 2

roaster_notes.note: P6 was returned for lack of a measured gain, which does not apply because this patch's gain is functional. P3's fd_set-internals concern applies to the FD_SETSIZE alternative in message #6, not to this patch.

From the standards and compatibility angle the proposal adds no syntax, option, GUC, catalog object or dump format, and existing pgbench scripts and option sets run unchanged on macOS. The only user-visible change is a higher client limit on that platform. I could not check from the material whether the pgbench documentation or the existing 'too many client connections for select()' error text names the limit and would need an update.

The patch changes only how pgbench waits on its own client sockets inside one process. It adds no on-disk format, WAL record, catalog entry, wire protocol message or backend ABI change. There is no persistent or cross-node state for this angle to judge.

The proposal has no privilege or exposure aspect. pgbench is a client tool that runs as the invoking OS user and opens only its own connections. A kqueue socket set changes how that process waits on its own sockets, and grants no server-side privilege, file access or view of other sessions. A larger client count per thread is bounded by the user's own rlimits and by max_connections on the server, as with ppoll() on Linux today.
Two fixable design and maintenance concerns. Costs stay inside pgbench on platforms without ppoll(), so nothing here is fatal.
Both objections are about desirability and simpler alternatives. The design mirrors kqueue use in waiteventset.c, which makes a fatal objection unlikely.
The cost is limited to pgbench on platforms without ppoll(), so this is a "not now, show demand" point rather than a rejection.
